ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the volar forearm at mid-forearm, roughly half its length.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Intermediate layer of the anterior compartment -- superficial to flexor digitorum profundus, deep to flexor carpi radialis and flexor carpi ulnaris.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Separate bellies for each digit can be resolved (FDS2-FDS5), which is what allows several to be injected in one needle pass.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: The in-plane technique is preferred here: FDS2, FDS3 and FDS5 can be reached at their points of maximum thickness in a single pass, cutting the number of punctures.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part I -- Distal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(3):107 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17030107

trigger_points.location_description: Bellies in the middle third of the volar forearm, superficial to flexor digitorum profundus, along lines from the medial epicondyle toward each finger.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Along the palmar aspect of the corresponding finger to the fingertip; the whole finger aches rather than the wrist. Finger stiffness and a locking sensation are reported by Travell and Simons.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Prolonged or forceful gripping (tools, steering, climbing), sudden overload.
trigger_points.notes: Non-myofascial differential: trigger finger, carpal tunnel syndrome, Dupuytren's disease, flexor tenosynovitis, cervical radiculopathy.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 38; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 38 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: FDS flexes the PIP joints independently (unlike FDP, whose tendons share a common belly), then the MCP joints and wrist; it is the main power source for the middle-phalanx grip. Its elbow flexion moment is small. At the elbow its clinically important role is as the second-ranked dynamic valgus stabiliser after FCU, with FCU+FDS co-contraction giving the greatest protection of the ulnar collateral ligament in cadaver loading; the humero-ulnar head's attachment to the sublime tubercle and ligament explains this. Tight FDS arch and hypertrophy contribute to proximal median neuropathy.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None at the elbow; the ulnar bursa (common flexor synovial sheath) surrounds the tendons at the wrist. Adjacent structures and relations: Median nerve (on the deep surface of FDS from the arch to the wrist), ulnar artery and nerve (between FDS and FDP medially), FDP deep, FCR/PL/FCU superficial, the anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament deep to the humero-ulnar head.

trigger_points.location: Proximal and mid-forearm bellies, deep to FCR/PL, identified by resisted PIP flexion of the corresponding finger; Travell & Simons map FDS and FDP TrPs together.
trigger_points.referred_pain: along the volar aspect of the finger served, to the fingertip (for example the middle finger, or the ring and little fingers together), described as lightning-like or deep; little proximal spread.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Finger pain and stiffness, weak grip, painful sustained gripping (steering wheel, tools); mistaken for trigger finger, flexor tenosynovitis or ulnar/median neuropathy; stiff, painful fingers in the morning. Entrapment: The FDS arch is a recognised median-nerve compression site (pronator syndrome, provoked by resisted middle-finger PIP flexion). Associated TrPs: FDP, FCR, FCU, palmaris longus, pronator teres, hand extensors (antagonists).

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi (ulnar fingers)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this territory (volar fingers) from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Medial epicondylar debridement and UCL reconstruction pass through or beneath the FDS/flexor–pronator origin; preserving it maintains the dynamic stabiliser. Test each FDS slip individually; assume the little finger slip may be absent.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.
sources: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., 2021: flexor digitorum superficialis; median nerve.
Park MC, Ahmad CS. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2004;86(10):2268–2274.
Johnson RK, Spinner M, Shrewsbury MM. J Hand Surg Am 1979;4(1):48–51.
Johnson RK, Spinner M, Shrewsbury MM. Median nerve entrapment syndrome in the proximal forearm. J Hand Surg Am. 1979;4(1):48–51.

Zwerus EL, Somford MP, Maissan F, Heisen J, Eygendaal D, van den Bekerom MPJ. Physical examination of the elbow, what is the evidence? A systematic literature review. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(19):1253–1260.

tests.name: Resisted middle-finger PIP flexion (FDS arch provocation)
tests.performance: Site-specific provocation: resisted pronation with the elbow extending loads the pronator teres heads; resisted elbow flexion–supination loads the lacertus fibrosus; resisted middle-finger PIP flexion loads the FDS arch (Johnson, Spinner & Shrewsbury 1979). Thenar-palm numbness (palmar cutaneous branch) and absence of nocturnal predominance separate it from carpal tunnel syndrome. No validated sensitivity/specificity data have been published for these manoeuvres; this is stated rather than estimated.
tests.accuracy: No validated sensitivity/specificity data have been published for these manoeuvres; this is stated rather than estimated.
tests.source: Johnson RK, Spinner M, Shrewsbury MM. Median nerve entrapment syndrome in the proximal forearm. J Hand Surg Am. 1979;4(1):48–51.

clinical.tests_caveat: Values are taken from the cited primary studies. Most series are small and reference standards differ (surgery, arthroscopy, electrodiagnostics), so treat the numbers as indicative. The systematic review of Zwerus et al. (2018) found 24 described elbow tests, only 14 with any accuracy data, and concluded that no single test can rule an elbow diagnosis in or out on its own. Where no accuracy data exist, this is stated rather than estimated.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); wrist_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 31/08/2026. Sources. Gray's Anatomy 42nd ed. (2021) for attachments, innervation (root values as given by Gray's) and vascular supply; Travell, Simons & Simons' Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed. (1999, Vol. 1) and 3rd ed. (2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Flexion of the PIP joints of digits 2–5 (with relatively independent action of each tendon), then MCP flexion [1, 4]. At the wrist: Wrist flexion as an extrinsic flexor, most evident when the fingers are held extended; because FDS and FDP account for most of the flexor-side PCSA (total flexor PCSA about 21 cm² against about 11 cm² for the extensors), their combined wrist-flexion potential exceeds that of the prime flexors [9, 12]. Length–tension and grip: Grip force depends on wrist position through the length–tension relation of the digital flexors; it peaks near 30–35° extension [23]. Wrist flexion slackens the extrinsic flexors (tenodesis) [5]. Importance: Power grip; the ring-finger FDS is a standard donor (opponensplasty, FDS-to-FDP transfers) with limited donor deficit [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: Ulnar bursa from about 2–3 cm proximal to the retinaculum to the mid-palm, continuous with the little finger's digital sheath; communicates with the radial bursa (FPL) at the wrist in a proportion of hands, the anatomical basis of the horseshoe abscess [1, 4] [grade B]. Relations: The median nerve lies deep to FDS between FDS and FDP, emerging along its radial border in the distal forearm to lie between FDS and FCR at the wrist; the ulnar nerve and artery lie deep to FCU on the ulnar side of FDS [1]. Coupled structures: Median nerve (FDS arch proximally, carpal tunnel distally), ulnar artery, A1 pulley (trigger finger), Camper's chiasm [1, 4, 42, 44].

trigger_points.location: Bellies in the middle third of the volar forearm, superficial to FDP, along lines from the medial epicondyle toward each finger [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Along the palmar aspect of the corresponding finger to the fingertip; the whole finger aches rather than the wrist. Finger stiffness and a locking sensation are reported by Travell and Simons [grade B] [2, 3].
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Prolonged or forceful gripping (tools, steering, climbing), sudden overload [2, 3].

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior (ulnar palm, 4th–5th fingers)
scalenes and first dorsal interosseous (index finger)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred into FDS territory (palmar fingers and palm)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: Trigger finger, carpal tunnel syndrome, Dupuytren's disease, flexor tenosynovitis, cervical radiculopathy.
clinical.notes: Pronator syndrome includes median-nerve compression at the FDS arch [42]. Flexor tenosynovitis in the carpal tunnel raises canal pressure, which also rises with wrist flexion and extension [44]. Trigger finger arises at the A1 pulley; the FDS test isolates PIP flexion; flexor tendon zones and Camper's chiasm govern repair strategy [4].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
